title: Edit Distance
statement: You get two words. In one step you may insert a letter, delete a letter, or replace a letter. Return the smallest number of steps that turns the first word into the second. Either word may be empty.

example.caption: abc becomes yabd with two edits: put a y in front, and change the c into a d.

idea.sentence: Let dp[i][j] be the fewest edits for the first i letters of word1 and the first j letters of word2; a match copies the diagonal, a mismatch costs 1 plus the cheapest of the three neighbours.

jargon.plain: The first i letters of a word. The empty prefix has i = 0.
A grid where each cell stores the answer to a smaller version of the problem, so a bigger answer is built from cells already filled.

watch.inputHint: Two words (strings). Keep them short, each cell is one step and the trace stops at 60 steps.

compare.bruteLabel: Try every choice for each letter
compare.unit: steps (brute force really grows as 3 to the power n, drawn as the closest shape)

rows.name: Plain recursion
rows.note: Every mismatch branches three ways and the same pair of prefixes is solved again and again.

rows.name: DP table
rows.note: Each of the (n+1)(m+1) cells is solved once from three cells already filled.

fast.takeaway: The table has one cell per pair of prefixes. Each cell looks at only three neighbours, so the work is the table size. Keeping just two rows would cut the space to O(m).

stages.title: Base row and column
stages.note: Row 0 and column 0 hold the cost against an empty word: i deletes or j inserts.

stages.title: Letters match
stages.note: No edit is needed, so the cell copies the diagonal cell dp[i-1][j-1].

stages.title: Letters differ
stages.note: One edit plus the cheapest of up (delete), left (insert) and diagonal (replace).

stages.title: Read the corner
stages.note: The last cell, dp[m][n], covers both whole words. That is the answer.

edges.title: One word is empty
edges.why: Only the base row or column is used. Three inserts, or three deletes the other way round.

edges.title: Both empty
edges.why: The table is 1 by 1 and holds dp[0][0] = 0. No loop runs, and that is correct.

edges.title: Swapped letters
edges.why: Two replaces. A swap is not one move here, so a solution that counts it as 1 is wrong.

edges.title: Equal words
edges.why: Every cell on the diagonal copies the cell before it, so the zeros slide down to the corner.

gotchas.text: The table is (m+1) by (n+1), not m by n. Cell i, j talks about prefixes, so the letters to compare are word1[i-1] and word2[j-1]. Mixing i and i-1 is the classic off-by-one.
Forget the base row and column and every cell on the edge reads garbage. Row 0 is 0..n and column 0 is 0..m.
new Array(m + 1).fill(new Array(n + 1).fill(0)) shares one row between all rows. Writing one cell would change every row. Use Array.from with a fresh array per row.
make([][]int, m+1) only makes the outer slice, every inner slice is nil. Allocate each row with make([]int, n+1) in a loop. The built-in min of three values needs Go 1.21 or newer.
word1[i-1] is a byte. That is right for ASCII letters, but a word with accents or emoji needs []rune(word1) first.

recap.key: dp[i][j] is the cost for the first i and first j letters. Equal letters copy the diagonal, else 1 + min(up, left, diagonal).
recap.complexity: Time O(n*m). Space O(n*m), or O(m) with two rows.
moves: Fill row 0 with j and column 0 with i
Else 1 + min(up, left, diagonal), then read dp[m][n]
